items.back: $\overline{∫}f=\inf_{P}U(P,f)$, $\underline{∫}f=\sup_{P}L(P,f)$. $f$ is Riemann integrable if they are equal.
Same with $Δα_{i}=α(x_{i})−α(x_{i−1})$ for an increasing $α$. Written $f∈\mathscr R(α)$.
$P^{*}⊇P$. The common refinement of $P_{1},P_{2}$ is $P_{1}∪P_{2}$.
$I(x)=0$ for $x≤0$, $1$ for $x>0$. Integrating against $I(x−s)$ evaluates at $s$.
$Λ(γ)=\sup_{P}Σ|γ(x_{i})−γ(x_{i−1})|$; rectifiable if finite.
If $P^{*}$ refines $P$: $L(P,f,α)≤L(P^{*},f,α)$ and $U(P^{*},f,α)≤U(P,f,α)$.
$\underline{∫}f\,dα≤\overline{∫}f\,dα$.
$f∈\mathscr R(α)$ iff for every $ε>0$ there is $P$ with $U(P,f,α)−L(P,f,α)<ε$.
items.note: The single most-used theorem in the chapter.

items.back: If $U−L<ε$ for $P$, then any choice of tags gives a sum within $ε$ of the integral.
If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, $f∈\mathscr R(α)$.
If $f$ is monotone and $α$ is continuous, $f∈\mathscr R(α)$.
A bounded $f$ with finitely many discontinuities, at none of which $α$ jumps, is in $\mathscr R(α)$.
items.note: Abbott Ch 7.6 upgrades this: bounded and continuous except on a set of measure zero.

items.back: If $f∈\mathscr R(α)$ with $m≤f≤M$ and $φ$ is continuous on $[m,M]$, then $φ∘f∈\mathscr R(α)$.
Linear; monotone ($f≤g ⇒ ∫f≤∫g$); additive over $[a,c]∪[c,b]$; $fg∈\mathscr R$; $|∫f\,dα|≤∫|f|\,dα$.
$∫f\,d I(x−s)=f(s)$ for $f$ continuous at $s$. With $α=Σc_{n}I(x−s_{n})$, $∫f\,dα=Σc_{n}f(s_{n})$.
If $α'∈\mathscr R$, then $∫f\,dα=∫f(x)α'(x)\,dx$ (one side exists iff the other does).
For $φ$ strictly increasing and continuous onto $[a,b]$: $∫_{A}^{B}g\,dβ=∫_{a}^{b}f\,dα$ with $g=f∘φ$, $β=α∘φ$.
If $f∈\mathscr R$ and $F(x)=∫_{a}^{x}f$, then $F$ is continuous (Lipschitz), and $F'(x_{0})=f(x_{0})$ wherever $f$ is continuous.
If $f∈\mathscr R$ and $F'=f$ on $[a,b]$, then $∫_{a}^{b}f=F(b)−F(a)$.
$∫_{a}^{b}Fg=F(b)G(b)−F(a)G(a)−∫_{a}^{b}fG$ when $F'=f$, $G'=g$ are integrable.
If $γ'$ is continuous, $γ$ is rectifiable and $Λ(γ)=∫_{a}^{b}|γ'(t)|\,dt$.

items.modelProof: Add one point $x^{*}$ to $[x_{i−1},x_{i}]$. The inf of $f$ on each half is at least $m_{i}$, so the lower sum can only grow. Induct on the number of added points.
($⇐$) $L(P)≤\underline{∫}≤\overline{∫}≤U(P)$, so $0≤\overline{∫}−\underline{∫}<ε$ for every $ε$. ($⇒$) Pick $P_{1},P_{2}$ with $U(P_{2})<∫+ε/2$ and $L(P_{1})>∫−ε/2$, and use the common refinement.
$f$ is uniformly continuous on $[a,b]$ (4.19). Choose $η$ with $[α(b)−α(a)]η<ε$ and $δ$ so that $|x−t|<δ ⇒ |f(x)−f(t)|<η$. For $Δx_{i}<δ$, $M_{i}−m_{i}≤η$, so $U−L≤ηΣΔα_{i}<ε$.

items.prompt: Prove: $F$ is continuous and $F'=f$ at continuity points.
items.modelProof: $|F(y)−F(x)|≤M|y−x|$ with $M=\sup|f|$. At a continuity point $x_{0}$: $\left|\dfrac{F(t)−F(s)}{t−s}−f(x_{0})\right|=\left|\dfrac{1}{t−s}∫_{s}^{t}(f(u)−f(x_{0}))du\right|<ε$ when $s,t$ are within $δ$ of $x_{0}$.

For any partition, the MVT gives $t_{i}$ with $F(x_{i})−F(x_{i−1})=f(t_{i})Δx_{i}$. Summing, $F(b)−F(a)=Σf(t_{i})Δx_{i}$, which lies between $L(P)$ and $U(P)$. Since $f∈\mathscr R$, those squeeze to $∫f$.

items.hint: Use the uniform partition with $n$ pieces.

items.prompt: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, prove $∫_{a}^{b}f=f(c)(b−a)$ for some $c$.
items.modelProof: With $m,M$ the min and max, $m(b−a)≤∫f≤M(b−a)$. The average lies in $[m,M]$, and IVT gives $c$ with $f(c)$ equal to it.

items.prompt: A bounded function on $[a,b]$ that is continuous except at countably many points is Riemann integrable.
items.explanation: Countable sets have measure zero; Lebesgue's criterion (A 7.6.5, Rudin 11.33).
If $f(c)>0$, continuity keeps $f>f(c)/2$ on an interval, making the integral positive.

items.prompt: Changing $f$ at one point doesn't change integrability or the integral.
items.explanation: The difference is 0 except at one point; its upper sums can be made small.

items.claim: The Dirichlet function is Riemann integrable on $[0,1]$ with integral 0.
lines: The rationals are countable, so they take up no length.
$f=0$ everywhere except on a set that doesn't matter.
items.explanation: Upper sums use the sup on each subinterval, and every subinterval contains rationals, so $U(P)=1$ for every $P$. “Countable sets don't matter” is true for the Lebesgue integral, not the Riemann integral.

lines: The sum telescopes, so every Riemann sum equals $F(b)−F(a)$.
items.explanation: MVT produces particular tags $t_{i}$, not arbitrary ones, and nothing guarantees $f$ is integrable. Rudin assumes $f∈\mathscr R$ in 6.21. $F=x^{2}\sin(1/x^{2})$ breaks the claim.

lines: By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $∫_{−1}^{1}f=F(1)−F(−1)$.
items.explanation: $x^{−2}$ is unbounded on $[−1,1]$, so it is not Riemann integrable, and $F'=f$ fails at 0. (A positive function with a negative integral is a warning sign.)

items.name: Dirichlet function $1_{Q}$ on $[0,1]$
items.details: Every $U=1$, every $L=0$: not Riemann integrable. (It is Lebesgue integrable with integral 0; Chapter 11.)

items.name: Thomae's function
items.details: Integrable with integral 0 even though it is discontinuous at every rational (its discontinuities have measure zero).

items.name: $2·1_{Q}−1$
items.details: $f^{2}≡1$ and $|f|≡1$ are integrable, but $f$ is not.

items.name: $F(x)=x^{2}\sin(1/x^{2})$, $F(0)=0$
items.details: $F$ is differentiable on $[0,1]$ but $F'$ is unbounded, so $F'∉\mathscr R$. FTC needs its hypothesis.

items.name: $\mathrm{sgn}(x)$ on $[−1,1]$
items.details: Integrable, but $F(x)=∫_{−1}^{x}\mathrm{sgn}=|x|−1$ is not differentiable at 0.
